headline: T-wave inversion on the ECG is found in about 4% of adult athletes; its link to later heart events is unclear
question: How often do athletes show T-wave inversion (TWI) on a resting ECG, and does it predict heart disease or heart events?
design: A systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, registered in PROSPERO) of studies reporting how often athletes of any sport, sex, ethnicity or age show TWI, or what lay behind it. Data came from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. Of 4,509 articles found, 115 were included. The prevalence question used 110 studies with 258,954 people in all: that total is the n on this card. The other questions used far fewer athletes with TWI: 34 studies looked for heart disease behind it and 20 followed athletes for heart events. Twelve studies were left out of the pooling because their TWI definition was not standard; 42 used the International (Seattle) criteria and 32 the ESC criteria. Studies were cross-sectional or cohort studies; risk of bias was rated with the Joanna Briggs checklist (53 adequate, 31 unclear, 26 inadequate). Random-effects models gave pooled prevalence, with checks by sex, age, ethnicity and ECG criteria.
findings:
Athletes over 16 years, International criteria: pooled TWI prevalence 4% (95% CI 3 to 6%; single studies 0 to 42%): 3% in anterior, 1% in inferior and 0% in lateral leads. With ESC criteria it was also 4%. Studies of older athletes found more TWI.

Black athletes 13% vs Caucasian athletes 3%; women 7% vs men 5%.

TWI was more common in athletes than in non-athletes (14 studies; prevalence ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.97).

Structural heart disease among athletes with TWI (34 studies): under 1% in 19 studies, 1 to 10% in 9 and over 10% in 6. Lateral-lead TWI was most often linked to cardiomyopathy. During follow-up, new diagnoses ran at 0 to 55 per 1,000 athletes per year (13 studies) and heart events at 0 to 83 per 1,000 per year (20 studies).
limits: Heterogeneity was very high: I² above 80% in most analyses and single studies from 0 to 42%, so the pooled 4% hides large differences between studies. Funnel plots suggested publication bias or this heterogeneity. A quarter of the prevalence studies (26 of 110) were rated inadequate for risk of bias. The studies were observational, mixed in who was screened and how, and used different tests to look for heart disease. Follow-up studies were small and short, and the authors say they had too little power to judge the risk of heart events. Rates from 0 to 83 events and 0 to 55 new diagnoses per 1,000 per year show how unstable those figures are. Athlete status, sport and age differed between studies. Selection and referral bias are likely, since people with an odd ECG are the ones sent for follow-up. The review was partly funded by a public research network (CIBERCV, Instituto de Salud Carlos III); the authors declare no competing interests. The authors' conclusion is careful and matches the numbers.
meaning: The heart lessons (heart-grey-zone, heart-scd) teach that training changes the ECG, but that some findings, such as T-wave inversion, need a full work-up: history, ECG, echo and sometimes MRI. This review fits: TWI is uncommon, more frequent in athletes, and most athletes with it have no cardiomyopathy, yet some do. It does not show who is at risk. A pooled prevalence from very mixed studies (I² above 80%) is one reason to rank it low (ev-pyramid). The lessons stand.

variants.stem: A club doctor screens 500 adult athletes with the International criteria. About how many show T-wave inversion, going by the 2026 meta-analysis?

options.why: Right: the pooled prevalence was 4% (95% CI 3 to 6%), so about 20 of 500, though studies varied widely.
That is far above the pooled 4%.
That is ten times too low; it may come from reading the 0% lateral-lead figure as the total.

options.text: None; TWI only occurs in people with heart disease
options.why: TWI was more common in athletes than in non-athletes (prevalence ratio 1.49), and most athletes with it had no cardiomyopathy.

variants.stem: Most athletes with TWI in the 2026 meta-analysis had no cardiomyopathy. What follows?

options.text: Often benign, but a full work-up is still needed to find those with disease
options.why: Right: in 19 of 34 studies under 1% had structural heart disease, but in 6 it was over 10%, and the authors say thorough evaluation is essential.

options.text: TWI is harmless and needs no follow-up in athletes
options.why: Some athletes with TWI had cardiomyopathy, especially with lateral-lead TWI, and the authors urge a thorough evaluation.

options.text: TWI proves an athlete's heart has remodelled from training
options.why: It may reflect remodelling, but the review cannot tell this from disease on the ECG alone.

options.text: TWI predicts sudden cardiac death in every athlete who has it
options.why: The review found event risk uncertain, with low power and high heterogeneity.
